title: Iran at the Crossroads — Eddie Would Go
units: Politics · 12 min read
Iran at the Crossroads
Tehran navigates between international pressure and its own internal contradictions. With nuclear negotiations stalled and an economy at breaking point, the regime faces a historic crossroads.
20 March 2026 · Politics

"The regime which is destroyed by a revolution is almost always an improvement on its immediate predecessor, and experience teaches us that the most dangerous moment for a bad government is generally that in which it sets about reform."
— "The Old Regime and the Revolution" - Alexis de Tocqueville

The streets of Tehran are burning again, but this time the fire is different. What began as another protest over accelerating inflation has rapidly turned into a collective cry questioning the very foundations of the Islamic Republic. Young women burn their veils in front of phone cameras, traders shut their doors in the Grand Bazaar, and graffiti appears on walls demanding not reform but the end of the regime. This is no passing discontent; it is the symptom of a prolonged illness: a total divorce between an ageing state and a young society that no longer believes in it. A divorce caused by a militarised political economy that has broken the social contract and the promises of the 1979 revolution.

Iran today suffers a gulf between its social dynamics and a state and institutional structure anchored in the past. The Iranian population is one of the youngest (median age: 32), most urbanised (more than 75% live in cities) and most educated (a literacy rate above 85%, with university enrolment in which women exceed 60%) in the Middle East. This society is globally connected through social media and VPNs, consuming culture and news from abroad. Yet it is governed by an ideological, gerontocratic and centralised political system in which key decisions rest with an unelected supreme figure and with closed institutions such as the Guardian Council. This structural tension — a modern, diverse society aspiring to individual freedoms, imprisoned by a theocratic state — is one of the fundamental engines of this permanent conflict. The protests are not mere economic outbursts but the recurring expression of this systemic incompatibility.
1. The evolution of protest: from reformism to rupture

What makes these protests different from earlier ones? Images of demonstrations against the Iranian regime are nothing new. Criticism of the system has existed since it consolidated its most extreme turn in the early 1980s. The first more intense episode of protest came in 2009, after the presidential elections — the so-called Green Movement — when the re-election of Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, against more moderate candidates such as the cleric Karroubi and the candidate Hossein Mousavi, led the urban middle classes in particular to question the legitimacy of the vote. Those protests, however, were reformist in character. Everyone politically involved in the Green Movement was part of the establishment: they demanded reform and a rapprochement with the West, not a political revolution.

The next focus of protest came between 2017 and 2018, with a clear economic backdrop, the product of the elimination of subsidies and rising food prices. It was then that press reports began to register a crucial shift in the slogans: demands for reform gave way to demands for radical change; criticism of the electoral system turned into direct challenges to the Revolutionary Guard. The protests also spread beyond the major cities, reaching both rural areas and medium-sized towns.

The third great cycle of mobilisation erupted after the death of Mahsa Amini in September 2022, marking an unprecedented qualitative rupture in the history of the Islamic Republic. This episode transformed the earlier economic discontent into a cultural and feminist insurgency under the slogan "Woman, Life, Freedom" (Zan, Zendegi, Azadi). Unlike earlier movements, this wave was led by Generation Z and by young women who directly challenged the regime's most visible ideological pillar: the compulsory wearing of the hijab. The cultural and identity component mobilised young people, women and various ethnic minorities as never before, given that Mahsa Amini was of Kurdish origin.
2. The engine of discontent: economic crisis and social attrition

From 2009 onwards, the protests also took on growing criticism of Iranian foreign policy: the investment by the government and the Revolutionary Guard in actors such as Hezbollah, Bashar al-Assad's Syrian government and the Houthis in Yemen, while the population endures hardship, galloping inflation, a collapsed health system, falling real incomes and water shortages in the major cities. The contrast between excessive spending on regional projects and precariousness at home has become one of the principal triggers of discontent.

Iran's economy has passed through what the World Bank calls a "lost decade", marked by volatile growth and a systematic erosion of welfare. After sanctions were reimposed in 2018, GDP contracted by around 12% in two years, then recovered at mediocre annual rates of 2–3%, insufficient to return to 2017 levels. Oil exports fell from a peak of 2.5 million barrels a day to fewer than 400,000, generating a chronic fiscal deficit financed by money printing. Poverty went from affecting 22% of the population in 2017 to more than 33% in 2023, pushing almost 10 million people below the extreme poverty line. Productivity, for its part, has fallen steadily owing to the lack of foreign investment and to technological isolation.

To understand the current explosion it is essential to examine the reform of the subsidy system and the unification of exchange rates. For years Iran operated multiple exchange rates to protect its economy. In an attempt to correct these distortions and put the fiscal accounts in order, the government announced a surprise increase in the price of petrol from 10,000 to 30,000 rials per litre (up to 300%). This drove year-on-year inflation above 41%, with peaks of 70% for food in the peripheral provinces. The direct compensation offered by the state amounted to some four dollars at the real exchange rate and was absorbed by inflation in less than a quarter. And the unification of the exchange rate harmed bazaar owners relative to business conglomerates tied to the regime.
3. The architecture of power: an armoured system

This economic collapse unfolds atop a political system of dual power, designed around the concept of Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist). At its summit stands the Supreme Leader, with lifetime command over the armed forces and the judiciary, and broad powers of veto. Both the president and the parliament are elected by popular vote, but the system's real filter is the Guardian Council, an unelected 12-member body — half appointed directly by the Supreme Leader and half by the head of the judiciary, who is himself named by the Leader. This council has the power to disqualify candidates before any election, ensuring that only those loyal to the principles of the revolution can compete.

The system's enforcement arm is the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), an organisation that not only controls security but administers a vast business empire. Through economic holdings such as the Khatam al-Anbiya conglomerate, it controls strategic sectors representing, according to estimates by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), between 20% and 40% of Iran's total GDP. Its influence ranges from the construction of critical infrastructure (ports, dams, pipelines) and oil and gas extraction to telecommunications, banking, car manufacturing and a lucrative smuggling trade on the borders.

This "parallel economy" allows the regime to finance its survival even under extreme sanctions, though the cost of that institutional resilience is the definitive rupture of the social contract with its citizens. The regime's response to each wave of protest has combined severe repression — arrests, violence and harassment — with minimal concessions.
4. A broad coalition and an uncertain future

This new conjuncture has managed to overlay traditionally distinct actors: the merchant class of the bazaars, the urban middle and lower classes, women, the young, communities affected by water scarcity, and ethnic minorities. Together they form a coalition with a mobilising capacity recalling the one that in its day destabilised the Shah's government.

At the same time, this cycle of protest openly demands the fall of the regime and coincides, for the first time in decades, with the consolidation of an opposition leadership in exile headed by Reza Pahlavi, son of the last Shah. Pahlavi has managed to capitalise on part of the discontent and to project himself as an organised and recognisable voice among the diaspora and the population inside Iran. According to opinion surveys carried out by the Group for Analyzing and Measuring Attitudes in Iran (GAMAAN) in collaboration with the Iranian-American Research Institute (IRI), his favourability has come to hover around 30%. It is crucial to interpret these numbers with extreme caution, given how enormously difficult it is to conduct reliable polling in a country under an authoritarian regime.

These figures work, however, less as a precise measurement than as a significant political thermometer: they indicate that, for the first time in decades, a monarchical alternative to the Islamic Republic's system is achieving a tangible degree of resonance and has become an actor the regime cannot entirely ignore. His relative popularity does not predict a return to the throne, but it does mark a shift in the political imagination of part of the opposition, which is beginning to articulate demands not only for reform but for regime change, with a symbolic figure at its head.

All these factors make this wave of protest one of the greatest challenges the regime has faced in recent years. It is not clear, however, that it will lead to collapse or a change of government without a fracture within the repressive apparatus or the army. The most likely outcome, for now, is a cyclical repetition of protest and a drift towards anomie which — as the historian Robert Kaplan argues — tends to be worse for a population than any authoritarian regime. Such a scenario would also imply enormous instability for the whole region of the Middle East, Pakistan and Afghanistan.

At this moment it is impossible to predict Iran's future. It is worth recalling, however, Alexis de Tocqueville's warning: the most dangerous moment for an oppressive regime is when it attempts to reform itself, for every concession does nothing but illuminate the injustice of what still remains.
